record.paper_title: Open Problems in Human Trait Genetics
record.original_question: How can a significant statistical association between a genetic variant, gene, or locus and a complex human trait be converted into high-confidence causal evidence, despite linkage disequilibrium obscuring causal variants, limited experimentally validated causal benchmarks, and the need for formal standards for research or clinical causality claims?

evidence.quote: Even when a genomic locus is robustly established as causally linked to a phenotype, it is very difficult to tell with certainty which of the variants in that locus are behind that causal link, a task known as fine-mapping
it is still an open problem how to establish the causality of a variant or a gene with certainty (open problem #12: from association to causality).

An important factor limiting our progress towards established standards for causality is the shortage of confirmed, experimentally-validated causal variants that can be used as a gold standard for validation and evaluation of methods.

artifact.status_search_result: The conversion of statistical genetic association into high-confidence causal evidence (fine-mapping, causal gene identification, Mendelian randomization, formal causality standards) remains an active and unresolved area of research. Recent literature (2022–2025) on statistical fine-mapping (e.g., SuSiE, CARMA), functionally-informed methods, and benchmarking against experimentally validated variants continues to acknowledge the absence of a definitive framework and a comprehensive gold-standard set, indicating the problem is still open.

status_evidence.title: Fine-mapping from summary data with the Sum of Single Effects model (SuSiE-RSS)
status_evidence.snippet: Identifying causal variants from association studies is challenging due to LD; methods provide posterior inclusion probabilities but ground truth remains limited.
status_evidence.claim: Current state-of-the-art fine-mapping yields probabilistic candidates, not certainty, and lacks broad experimental gold standards.
